{{Short description|Immigration detention center in Texas, United States}}
{{Use American English|date=July 2025}}
The '''T. Don Hutto Residential Center''' (formerly known as '''T. Don Hutto Family Residential Facility''', and the '''T. Don Hutto Family Detention Facility'''<ref name=LIRS_2014/>) is a guarded, fenced-in, multi-purpose center currently used to detain foreign nationals awaiting the outcome of their immigration status. The center is located at 1001 Welch Street in the city of [[Taylor, Texas|Taylor]], [[Texas]], within [[Williamson County, Texas|Williamson County]]. Formerly a medium-security state prison, it is operated by [[CoreCivic]] under contract with the [[U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] agency (known as ICE) through an ICE {{interlanguage link|intergovernmental agreement|lt=Intergovernmental Service Agreement (IGSA)|pl|Porozumienie administracyjne}} with Williamson County, Texas.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.correctionscorp.com/facilitylist.cfm# | title = Facility Locations List | publisher = Corrections Corporation of America | accessdate = 2007-12-06 | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20071111122516/http://www.correctionscorp.com/facilitylist.cfm | archivedate = 2007-11-11 | url-status = dead }}</ref><ref>[http://www.ice.gov/news/library/factsheets/facilities-hutto.htm Don Hutto Family Residential Facility] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110622114102/http://www.ice.gov/news/library/factsheets/facilities-hutto.htm |date=2011-06-22 }}</ref> In 2006, Hutto became an immigrant-detention facility detaining immigrant families.<ref name="newyorker_2008">{{citation |url=http://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2008/03/03/the-lost-children |title=The Lost Children: What do tougher detention policies mean for illegal immigrant families? |author=Margaret Talbot |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |date=March 3, 2008 |accessdate=February 13, 2017}}</ref>  The facility was turned into a women's detention center in 2009.<ref name="guardian2015">{{citation |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2015/oct/29/texas-immigration-detention-center-women-hunger-strike |title=More than 20 women detained in Texas immigration facility begin hunger strike |author=Tom Dart |date=October 29, 2015 |accessdate=February 13, 2018 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref>

==History==
In July 1997, the T. Don Hutto Correctional Facility by was opened by CCA as a medium security prison.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cook |first=Terry |date=2018-06-28 |title=Terry Cook: The long road to T. Don Hutto |url=https://www.statesman.com/story/news/local/2018/06/28/terry-cook-the-long-road-to-t-don-hutto/10398386007/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Austin American-Statesman |language=en}}</ref> By 2000, Tennessee-based CCA's stocks hit their lowest, as it suffered from "poor management", prison riots and escapes. It had failed in the 1990s in its "bid to take over the entire prison system of Tennessee."<ref name="newyorker_2008" /> It is named after [[T. Don Hutto]], who along with [[Robert Crants (CEO)|Robert Crants]] and [[Thomas W. Beasley|Tom Beasley]], co-founded CCA on January 28, 1983 in Nashville, Tennessee.<ref name="harmon">{{cite journal |author=Harmon L. Wray, Jr. |url=http://southernchanges.digitalscholarship.emory.edu/sc08-3_1204/sc08-3_011/ |title=Cells for Sale |journal=Southern Changes: The Journal of the Southern Regional Council |volume=8 |number=3 |date=1989 |accessdate=February 13, 2017 |archive-date=February 14, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170214182512/http://southernchanges.digitalscholarship.emory.edu/sc08-3_1204/sc08-3_011/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="donnaselmanbigbusiness">{{cite book |author1=Donna Selman |author2=Paul Leighton |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qb3BAAAAQBAJ&q=%22corrections+corporation+of+America%22+%22vanderbilt+university%22&pg=PA81 |title=Punishment for Sale: Private Prisons, Big Business, and the Incarceration Binge |location=New York City |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield Publishers |date=2010|isbn = 9781442201743}}</ref>{{rp|81–2}}<ref>{{citation |url=http://tdhhistory.blogspot.ca/ |title=The history of T. Don Hutto |date=December 3, 2007 |accessdate=February 13, 2017}}</ref> In March 2004 CCA announced plans to close the facility, citing low inmate demand.<ref name="businesswire2004">{{citation |url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20040323005876/en/Corrections-Corporation-America-Announces-Contract-Resume-Management |title=Corrections Corporation of America Announces Contract to Resume Management of the Delta Correctional Facility and Closure of T. Don Hutto Correctional Center |date=March 23, 2004 |accessdate=August 28, 2018 |publisher=[[Business Wire]]}}</ref>

Immigration detention increased after 9/11.<ref name="newyorker_2008" /> In October 2005, [[Michael Chertoff]], then [[Secretary of Homeland Security]] under President [[George W. Bush]], said that [[U.S. Department of Homeland Security|DHS]] would "return every single illegal entrant" apprehended by U.S. authorities without exception and would make use of $90 million in funds appropriated by Congress to add additional beds in immigration detention facilities.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.foxnews.com/story/chertoff-end-catch-and-release-at-borders|title = Chertoff: End 'Catch and Release' at Borders|date = October 18, 2005|publisher = [[Associated Press]] via [[Fox News]]|access-date = July 18, 2015}}</ref> By July 2006, Chertoff told a House subcommittee that DHS had "achieved essentially 100 percent catch-and-remove."<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2006/jul/28/20060728-123022-6096r/?page=all|title = Chertoff hails end of let-go policy|date = July 28, 2006|accessdate = July 18, 2015|newspaper = [[Washington Times]]}}</ref> As a result, by the end of 2006, the number of people in government custody for immigration-law violations increased by 79% from 2005. There were about 14,000 people being detained.<ref name="newyorker_2008" />

T. Don Hutto re-opened in May 2006 as a "Family Residential Facility" to detain immigrant families.<ref>{{citation |url=http://www.ice.gov/pi/news/factsheets/huttofactsheet.htm |title=The ICE T. Don Hutto Family Residential Facility: maintaining family unity, enforcing immigration laws |publisher=[[U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] |date=April 2007 |accessdate=April 20, 2009 |archive-date=May 5, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090505234527/http://www.ice.gov/pi/news/factsheets/huttofactsheet.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> Previously, illegal immigrants with children would be released with a notice to appear before an immigration judge.  In some cases, where release was not approved by ICE, children were separated from their parents.  Parents were sent to an adult facility while children were released to family, or sent to the [https://web.archive.org/web/20160728223534/http://www.acf.hhs.gov/orr/programs/ucs Office of Refugee Resettlement.]

A 2007 report entitled [https://www.womensrefugeecommission.org/component/zdocs/document/150-locking-up-family-values-the-detention-of-immigrant-families-locking-up-family-values-the-detention-of-immigrant-families "Locking Up Family Values"] by the [[Women's Refugee Commission]] and [[Global Refuge|Lutheran Immigration and Refugee Services]] documented conditions in the facility.  The detainees were women and their children - most of whom appeared to be under the age of 12.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Women’s Commission for Refugee Women and Children |title=LOCKING UP FAMILY VALUES: The Detention of Immigrant Families |date=February 2007 |isbn=978-1-58030-058-2 |page=2 |url=https://www.womensrefugeecommission.org/images/zdocs/famdeten.pdf |accessdate=9 September 2018}}</ref> The report noted that most of the residents were from Central and South America. However, there were also Africans, Asians, Europeans, and Middle Easterners.  Many of the families held at the Hutto facility were awaiting adjudication of their claims for relief or asylum. Many of these families of the families held at the former prison are charged with no offenses other than [[illegal entry]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Women’s Commission for Refugee Women and Children |title=LOCKING UP FAMILY VALUES: The Detention of Immigrant Families |date=February 2007 |isbn=978-1-58030-058-2 |page=11 |url=https://www.womensrefugeecommission.org/images/zdocs/famdeten.pdf |accessdate=9 September 2018}}</ref>

The [[American Civil Liberties Union]] filed a lawsuit against ICE in March 2007 on behalf of 10 juvenile plaintiffs that were housed in the facility at the time claiming that the standards by which they were housed was not in compliance with the government's detention standards for this population.  The claims were, amongst other things, improper educational opportunities, inadequate privacy, and substandard health care.  The relief being sought was the release of the plaintiffs.  In August 2007, after the plaintiffs were no longer housed at the facility, the ACLU settled the lawsuit claiming that the situations at the facility had "significantly improved".<ref name="ACLU_2007" />

In 2007, Justice Sam Sparks approved the settlement between the ACLU and ICE that greatly improved conditions for immigrant children and their families who were detained at the facility. Dozens of children were released with their families as a result of the settlement.<ref name="ACLU_2007">{{cite web | url = https://www.aclu.org/immigrants/detention/31469prs20070827.html | title = Landmark Settlement Announced in Federal Lawsuit Challenging Conditions at Immigrant Detention Center in Texas | publisher = [[American Civil Liberties Union]] | date = August 27, 2007 | accessdate = December 6, 2007}}</ref> In response to the harsh treatment of young children in T. Don Hutto, Judge Sparks established "the government would have to establish clear rules for how to detain families safely and humanely. And although officials at Hutto might be making changes now, he noted, didn't Lawrence have a feeling it was merely because the defendants knew, on account of the lawsuit, that 'the hammer was coming down'?" He said that he was beginning to wonder who was in charge "out there, either C.C.A. or the government. It's very troubling to me."<ref name="newyorker_2008"/>

[http://theleastofthese-film.com/ The Least of These] is a documentary based on the lawsuit and sub-par conditions.<ref name="ACLU_2007_D">{{cite web | url = https://www.aclu.org/immigrants/detention/31469prs20070827.html | title = Landmark Settlement Announced in Federal Lawsuit Challenging Conditions at Immigrant Detention Center in Texas | publisher = American Civil Liberties Union | date = August 27, 2007 | accessdate = December 6, 2007}}</ref>

"[A]fter years of controversy, media exposure, and a lawsuit", in 2009, the Obama Administration closed T. Don Hutto Family Detention Facility, the United States’ "largest family immigration detention facility." "Conditions at the T. Don Hutto Family Detention Facility, and the impact of detention on families and children, proved that family detention could not be carried out humanely."<ref name="LIRS_2014">{{citation |url=http://lirs.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/LIRSWRC_LockingUpFamilyValuesAgain_Report_141114.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170214183442/http://lirs.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/LIRSWRC_LockingUpFamilyValuesAgain_Report_141114.pdf |archive-date=14 February 2017 |title=Locking Up Family Values, Again |date=October 2014 |accessdate=February 14, 2017 |pages=31 |publisher=[[Lutheran Immigration and Refugee Service]] and Women’s Refugee Commission |quote=Conditions at the T. Don Hutto Family Detention Facility, and the impact of detention on families and children, proved that family detention could not be carried out humanely}}</ref>{{rp|6}} On August 6, 2009, federal officials announced that T. Don Hutto would no longer house immigrant families.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Families no longer behind bars |first=Emily |last=Boswell |date=August 7, 2009 |access-date=June 21, 2018 |url=http://taylorpress.net/news/article_c469c652-950a-5288-956d-710ec14263e2.html |publisher=Taylor Press}}</ref> Instead, only female detainees will be housed there. ICE and [[Williamson County, Texas|Williamson County]] entered into a new contract, changing the facility to a non-criminal women's only detention center.<ref name="austinamericanstatesman2018">{{citation |author=Terry Cook |title=Terry Cook: The long road to T. Don Hutto |date=July 1, 2018 |url=https://www.statesman.com/news/local/terry-cook-the-long-road-don-hutto/pgVrNbkS6zQaOO5ypLS6uL/ |publisher=[[Austin American Statesman]] |accessdate=August 28, 2018}}</ref>  In September 2009, the last families left the facility and were moved to the much smaller Berks Family Residential Center in [[Pennsylvania]].<ref>[http://www.news8austin.com/content/your_news/default.asp?ArID=252912 Final families removed from T. Don Hutto facility]{{Dead link|date=October 2010}}</ref><ref>[https://www.ice.gov/factsheets/2009detention-reform ICE 2009 Detention Reform Fact Sheet]</ref>

In 2010 a former supervisor at T. Don Hutto was arrested on charges related to alleged sexual assault at the Detention Facility he was convicted of 5 misdemeanor charges.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rosetty |first1=Tricia |title=Former T. Don Hutto worker sentenced |url=http://taylorpress.net/news/taylor/article_a6e6c6dc-ec65-11df-bbfa-001cc4c002e0.html |accessdate=9 September 2018 |publisher=Taylor Press |date=Nov 10, 2010}}</ref>

In 2017 the FBI initiated a civil rights investigation against the center following allegations of guards sexually assaulting and sexually harassing detainees, and retaliation against those who filed complaints about the abuse.<ref>{{citation |title=FBI investigating after detainee claims guard sexually assaulted her |publisher=Spectrum News |date=December 13, 2017 |author=Claire Ricke |url=http://spectrumlocalnews.com/tx/austin/news/2017/12/13/fbi-investigating-after-detainee-claims-guard-sexually-assaulted-her |accessdate= February 13, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{citation |title=More women accuse Hutto guards of sexual misconduct |publisher=Spectrum News |date=November 22, 2017 |author=Jeff Stensland |url=http://spectrumlocalnews.com/tx/san-antonio/news/2017/11/22/two-more-women-accuse-hutto-detention-center-guards-of-sexual-misconduct |accessdate =February 13, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{citation |title=Letter details sexual assault at T. Don Hutto Residential Center |publisher=Spectrum News |date=November 9, 2017 |author=Ashley McElroy |url=http://spectrumlocalnews.com/tx/austin/news/2017/11/09/letter-details-sexual-assault-at-t--don-hutto-residential-center.html |accessdate=February 13, 2018}}</ref>

Williamson County commissioners in Taylor voted 4-1 on June 25, 2018, in the wake of a crisis of immigrant detention of children separated from their mothers who had been taken into custody, to end its participation in an Intergovernmental Agreement (IGA) with CoreCivic, in 2019. The facility was holding some of those imprisoned mothers.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20180626212340/https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/texas-suburb-ends-contract-with-immigrant-detention-center/2018/06/26/b30beaa2-796e-11e8-ac4e-421ef7165923_story.html Texas suburb ends contract with immigrant detention center], ''[[Washington Post]]'', Paul J. Weber (AP), June 26, 2018. Retrieved June 27, 2018.</ref>
